title: Surviving Futures
lessons/leverage-u3-l1/steps/0/body: In futures too, your size comes from **risk**, not leverage: **position value = risk amount ÷ stop distance (in %)**. Leverage only decides how much of your balance gets tied up as margin.
lessons/leverage-u3-l1/steps/1/prompt: Your account is 2,000 USDT, you risk 1%, and your stop loss is 4% below your entry. What should your position value be?
lessons/leverage-u3-l1/steps/1/explanati: 20 ÷ 4% = 500 USDT. If your stop gets hit: 500 × 4% = 20 USDT, exactly 1% of your account.
lessons/leverage-u3-l1/steps/2/title: Liquidation must sit far beyond your stop
lessons/leverage-u3-l1/steps/2/body: Once you've worked out your size, pick a leverage that puts your **liquidation price far beyond your stop loss**. With a 2% stop, 50x leverage (liquidation at about 2%) means you might get liquidated **before your stop**; 5x (liquidation at about 20%) gives you a safe gap.
lessons/leverage-u3-l1/steps/2/tip: At a fixed size, lowering leverage doesn't change your loss at the stop; it just pushes liquidation further away.
lessons/leverage-u3-l1/steps/3/prompt: You went long from 60,000 at 50x and set your stop loss 2% lower (58,800). The "Liquidation" line is your liquidation price. What's wrong with this trade?
lessons/leverage-u3-l1/steps/3/options/0: Liquidation comes before the stop loss
lessons/leverage-u3-l1/steps/3/options/1: The stop loss is too close to the entry
lessons/leverage-u3-l1/steps/3/options/2: The entry is right under resistance
lessons/leverage-u3-l1/steps/3/explanati: At 50x, liquidation is about 2% below entry, and maintenance margin pulls it a bit higher still (around 59,100). So price liquidates you before it ever reaches your stop. The fix: lower leverage with the same size.
lessons/leverage-u3-l1/steps/4/prompt: Put the steps for opening a futures trade in order.
lessons/leverage-u3-l1/steps/4/items/0: Find a logical stop loss spot on the chart
lessons/leverage-u3-l1/steps/4/items/1: Work out position value from your risk
lessons/leverage-u3-l1/steps/4/items/2: Choose leverage with liquidation far from the stop
lessons/leverage-u3-l1/steps/4/items/3: Place the order with a stop loss
lessons/leverage-u3-l1/steps/4/explanati: The chart decides where your stop goes; size comes from your risk and stop distance; leverage gets chosen last; and an order never goes in without a stop loss.
lessons/leverage-u3-l1/steps/5/statement: If you sized your position correctly from your risk, choosing 5x instead of 20x doesn't change your loss if the stop gets hit.
lessons/leverage-u3-l1/steps/5/explanati: Loss = position value × stop distance. Leverage only changes the margin tied up and the distance to liquidation, not this math.
lessons/leverage-u3-l1/steps/6/prompt: Which statement about high leverage is true?
lessons/leverage-u3-l1/steps/6/options/0: It moves the liquidation price closer to your entry
lessons/leverage-u3-l1/steps/6/options/1: It moves the liquidation price away from your entry
lessons/leverage-u3-l1/steps/6/options/2: It always earns you more profit
lessons/leverage-u3-l1/steps/6/explanati: The higher the leverage, the less margin and the shorter the distance from entry to liquidation, which leaves less room for normal market swings.
lessons/leverage-u3-l1/steps/7/sentence: With a 1,000 USDT account, 10 USDT risk and a 1% stop, your position value is ___ USDT, and at 5x the margin needed is ___ USDT.
lessons/leverage-u3-l1/steps/7/explanati: 10 ÷ 1% = 1,000 USDT position value; 1,000 ÷ 5 = 200 USDT margin. The account's effective leverage is 1x.
lessons/leverage-u3-l2/steps/0/body: When a long gets liquidated, the exchange's system closes it **by selling** (and closes shorts by buying). So every liquidation is itself an **extra order in the direction of the move**.
lessons/leverage-u3-l2/steps/1/body: If lots of leveraged longs have liquidation prices close together, the first drop liquidates a few of them, the forced selling pushes price lower, and **the next liquidations** kick in. The result: a sharp drop with a **long wick** and **very high volume**.
lessons/leverage-u3-l2/steps/2/prompt: Tap the candle where a cascade of long liquidations most likely happened.
lessons/leverage-u3-l2/steps/2/explanati: A sudden drop, far bigger than the candles before it, with a long lower wick and several times the volume. Back-to-back forced sells threw price down, and once the liquidations ran out, price bounced a little.
lessons/leverage-u3-l2/steps/3/title: Cascade fuel: open interest and funding
lessons/leverage-u3-l2/steps/3/body: **Open interest** is the total value of open contracts. High open interest together with **very positive funding** means lots of leveraged longs are in the market. The opposite (lots of shorts and negative funding) can lead to a **short squeeze**: a sharp rally as shorts get liquidated.
lessons/leverage-u3-l2/steps/4/prompt: In which situation is a cascade of long liquidations more likely?
lessons/leverage-u3-l2/steps/4/options/0: Very positive funding and open interest at a peak
lessons/leverage-u3-l2/steps/4/options/1: Negative funding and very low open interest
lessons/leverage-u3-l2/steps/4/options/2: A spot market with no leverage at all
lessons/leverage-u3-l2/steps/4/options/3: After most longs have already closed
lessons/leverage-u3-l2/steps/4/explanati: Positive funding and high open interest mean lots of leveraged longs with different liquidation prices are in the market: plenty of fuel for a chain-reaction drop.
lessons/leverage-u3-l2/steps/5/statement: Longs get liquidated through forced selling, which can make a price drop sharper.
lessons/leverage-u3-l2/steps/5/explanati: Every liquidated long is one extra sell order. If there are many, the drop feeds itself.
lessons/leverage-u3-l2/steps/6/statement: A short squeeze means price falls fast as shorts get liquidated one after another.
lessons/leverage-u3-l2/steps/6/explanati: Shorts get liquidated through forced buying, so a short squeeze means a sharp price rise, not a drop.
lessons/leverage-u3-l2/steps/7/prompt: How do you avoid becoming fuel for the next cascade?
lessons/leverage-u3-l2/steps/7/options/0: Use low leverage so your liquidation stays far from sharp swings
lessons/leverage-u3-l2/steps/7/options/1: Remove your stop loss so wicks don't knock you out
lessons/leverage-u3-l2/steps/7/options/2: Go in at 100x to profit faster
lessons/leverage-u3-l2/steps/7/options/3: Put your whole balance on the line with cross margin
lessons/leverage-u3-l2/steps/7/explanati: In a cascade, the people who get liquidated are the ones whose liquidation is close. Low leverage and the right size mean one sharp wick won't empty your account.
lessons/leverage-u3-l2/steps/8/pairs/2/m: Sharp drop as longs get liquidated
lessons/leverage-u3-l2/steps/8/pairs/3/m: Sharp rally as shorts get liquidated
lessons/leverage-u3-l3/steps/0/body: Before every futures trade: **setup matches your plan**, **stop loss on the chart**, **size from your risk**, **leverage with a far liquidation**, **margin type**, and **funding and big news**. If any one of them fails, don't enter.
lessons/leverage-u3-l3/steps/0/example/r: Behind a level, on the chart
lessons/leverage-u3-l3/steps/1/prompt: Your account is 500 USDT and you want to go long BTC. Your stop is 2% lower and you risk 1%. Which setup is right?
lessons/leverage-u3-l3/steps/1/explanati: 5 ÷ 2% = 250 USDT. At 5x, liquidation is about 20% away. A 500 USDT position risks 2% of your account, and at 50x its liquidation sits almost on the stop; at 100x, liquidation (about 1%) comes before the stop.
lessons/leverage-u3-l3/steps/2/prompt: You went long ETH from 3,000 at 20x with isolated margin and no stop loss. Tap the candle that most likely liquidated your position.
lessons/leverage-u3-l3/steps/2/explanati: At 20x, liquidation is about 5% below entry (near 2,850, a bit higher in practice). The first candle to reach it is this one, with the long wick. The candle before only dropped about 3%. Price bounced afterward, but your position was already closed.
lessons/leverage-u3-l3/steps/3/statement: If funding is high and positive and you plan to hold a long for a few days, the funding cost should go into your profit target math.
lessons/leverage-u3-l3/steps/3/explanati: Funding repeats every period on the full position value. Over a few days, it can eat a good chunk of your profit target.
lessons/leverage-u3-l3/steps/4/body: Once the position is open: **don't move your stop further away**, **don't add margin** to dodge liquidation, and review your size before **big news** (like CPI). News volatility can reach all the way to your liquidation price.
lessons/leverage-u3-l3/steps/4/tip: The worst futures habit: adding margin to a losing position instead of accepting the stop loss.
lessons/leverage-u3-l3/steps/5/prompt: You have a 10x long with isolated margin, and price has come close to your stop. What do you do?
lessons/leverage-u3-l3/steps/5/options/0: Let the stop loss do its job, as planned
lessons/leverage-u3-l3/steps/5/options/1: Add margin to push liquidation further away
lessons/leverage-u3-l3/steps/5/options/2: Remove the stop so price can come back
lessons/leverage-u3-l3/steps/5/options/3: Double your size to improve your average
lessons/leverage-u3-l3/steps/5/explanati: Your stop loss is the point where you decided in advance that your analysis was wrong. The other options just turn a small, planned loss into a big, unplanned one.
lessons/leverage-u3-l3/steps/6/pairs/1/m: Chosen after working out your size
lessons/leverage-u3-l3/steps/6/pairs/3/m: A position's periodic cost or income
lessons/leverage-u3-l3/steps/7/sentence: Your stop loss should always trigger ___ the liquidation price, and you choose leverage ___ working out your size.
lessons/leverage-u3-l3/steps/7/explanati: Your stop has to close the trade before liquidation so the loss stays under control. And leverage is the last decision, not the first.
lessons/leverage-u3-l3/steps/8/statement: With cross margin at 100x, if you don't set a stop loss, your maximum loss is just the position's initial margin.
lessons/leverage-u3-l3/steps/8/explanati: In cross, your account's entire free balance backs the position. So without a stop loss, your loss can reach your whole futures balance.
